author: ChuckJones
title: Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) has taken on $122 billion in debt sinc
text:
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) has taken on $122 billion in debt since March 2013 to buy back stock. The company had to take on the debt since it has to use U.S. based cash to do this and because it has not generated enough profits in the U.S. along with the U.S. cash it already had. It is worthwhile to calculate the difference between what it cost the company to take on debt since it does earn interest or receive dividends on the cash it would have had to spend. 
SEC filings give us the details Apple reports an “other income/(expense)” line on its income statement. This is a combination of three separate items: Interest and dividend income, interest expense, and other expense, net, which are in its 10-Q and 10-K filings. While the figure on Apple’s income statement can fluctuate by hundreds of millions of dollars from quarter to quarter the Interest and dividend income and interest expense do not. 
In the filings Apple provides what rate of return it earns on its cash and investments, and over the past five years it has steadily increased. When you calculate the interest rate the company has earned on the average of the beginning and ending debt balances it has generated $5.1 billion in extra income. 
Fiscal 2013: 1.03% Fiscal 2014: 1.11% Fiscal 2015: 1.49% Fiscal 2016: 1.73% Fiscal 2017: 1.99% December 2017 quarter: 2.11% The company doesn’t provide a blended interest rate cost on its debt. To calculate that I use the interest expenses that are in the filings and divide it by an average of the beginning and ending debt balances. In total Apple has paid $5.8 billion in interest payments. 
Fiscal 2013: 1.6% Fiscal 2014: 1.47% Fiscal 2015: 1.47% Fiscal 2016: 1.92% Fiscal 2017: 2.29% December 2017 quarter: 2.47% By using the delta between what Apple earns on the cash it retains and the average debt we can calculate an estimate on how much it has actually cost the company to take on the debt. This is the net cost of Apple’s debt over the past five plus years. 
Fiscal 2013: $48 million Fiscal 2014: $94 million Fiscal 2015: Earned $10 million more than interest expense Fiscal 2016: $146 million Fiscal 2017: $306 million December 2017 quarter: $106 million The $690 million in net cost has allowed the company to decrease its share count from 6.62 billion to 5.16 billion, or 22%. Between March 2013 to today Apple’s shares have risen from $63 to $174. 
Overall the company buying back its shares looks to have been a pretty good investment. And from the company’s comments on its earnings call it plans to move to a zero net cash position, which I calculate could add $32 to its stock price .
